title: Hire an AI engineer or bring in help: which comes first?
description: Hire an AI engineer, bring in help, or both? Census data, our job-ad count and a BLS cost build show what to do first.
topic: Hiring an AI engineer vs bringing in help
shortTopic: Hire an AI engineer or bring in help
job: Hiring an AI engineer vs bringing in help
verdict: Prove one workflow first, then hire a lead to own it.[^14][^15]
Firms using AI train current staff far more often than they hire AI-trained staff: about 15% versus 1.3%.[^1][^2]
Non-tech firms your size rarely advertise for AI engineers: about 125 US ads in 30 days, by our count.[^3][^4]
One AI engineer costs about $205,000 to $275,000 a year with benefits, by our math from BLS pay data.[^5][^7]
Whoever you bring in, write the handover into the contract and name who owns it after launch.[^17][^18]

headings.what-it-is: Hire an AI engineer or bring in help: what is the real choice?
headings.faq: Questions buyers ask about hiring an AI engineer

summary: The choice: hire an AI engineer, bring in outside help, or both, and in what order.[^14] Few firms start with a hire; training staff and new workflows are far more common.[^1][^2] What makes it work is a named workflow, a measure and an owner, not the hire.[^16][^17]
walkAway: One workflow, picked and priced: what it costs today in hours, errors or cash.[^16][^19] RAND's most common root cause of failure is a misunderstood problem.[^16]
A before-and-after measure, set before anyone builds.[^19] RAND sees models tuned to the wrong metrics; Google's second rule is to design metrics first.[^16][^19]
A working pilot in your own systems, with a go-or-stop date about 90 days out.[^15] Mid-market top performers took about 90 days from pilot to full use, in a preliminary, self-reported study.[^15]
A job spec for your first AI hire, if the pilot shows you need one.[^14] Ng's playbook builds the in-house team after pilots; one IT leader's advice is to start with a lead.[^14]
A handover written into the contract: runbooks, test data and who owns the system after launch.[^17]
humanRole: Ops lead or process owner: owns the problem and the success measure.[^17] RAND's top fix is to make sure technical staff understand the purpose and the domain.[^16]
COO or division head: signs off on go-live and owns the risk call.[^17] The AI playbook from NIST, the US standards body, puts AI risk decisions with executive leadership.[^17]
Front-line staff: check AI output before it reaches a customer.[^18] Of firms using AI, 66% use it only to help people with tasks.[^1]
A named internal owner: runs the system after handover, and the AI hire works toward that owner's goal.[^17]

recipes.name: 1. About 40 to 150 staff, no engineers: prove one workflow, hire later
recipes.when: One painful workflow, no engineers on staff and no AI in production.[^1] Ng's playbook starts with pilots that show traction before building a team.[^14]
flow: COO: pick the workflow and say what it costs today
Outside advisor: rank two or three AI bets and write specs
Ops lead: set the before-and-after measure
Division head: give the builder one subject-matter expert for the pilot
IT partner or vendor: build the pilot from the specs
Front-line staff: check every AI output during the pilot
COO: go, change or stop at about day 90
recipes.cost: Zavient starts with a free 30-minute diagnostic, then a fixed-scope 30-day sprint, and the build is quoted per job.[^25] That buys advice and specs, not an engineer, so it is not like for like with a hire.[^25][^5]

recipes.name: 2. About 150 to 500 staff, some IT: outside help now, a lead alongside
recipes.when: A second and third use case are queued, and an IT or data person can host the work. Partner-led pilots reached deployment about twice as often as internal builds; the study calls that correlation, not cause.[^15]
flow: COO: approve the role, the budget and the first workflow
Outside advisor: run the first workflow and write the AI lead's job spec
HR lead: recruit, planning for 39 to 75 days with the seat empty
New AI lead: build with the advisor, then own the system
Ops lead: own the measure, and roll out at one site or team first
Controller: track spend against the measured gain
recipes.cost: The hire runs about $205,000 to $275,000 a year with benefits, by our math from BLS pay data.[^5][^7] Zavient advisory can run alongside, but it is not like for like, since advice is not engineering.[^25]

recipes.name: 3. Any size, everyday tasks: make the team you have better
recipes.when: The gain is staff using AI tools in daily work, not a custom system.[^1] Lightcast found 51% of job ads asking for AI skills are outside IT.[^13]
flow: Division head: name three to five tasks per team to try
Team leads: train staff and set rules on what data goes in
Staff: use the tools and log time saved and errors
Ops lead: review the log monthly and stop what doesn't help
recipes.cost: Staff time and tool licences, with no new hire. By our math, training current staff is more than ten times as common as hiring AI-trained staff.[^1][^2]

ownData.title: Who actually posts AI-engineer jobs: firms your size, or giants?
ownData.intro: We counted US job ads for AI and machine learning engineers posted in the 30 days to 26 Nov 2026, by employer size and industry.[^3][^4] Operating firms of 51 to 500 staff posted about 125, against 1,262 from the largest firms in the same sectors.[^3] So a first in-house AI engineer is rare at firms your size, which matches the Census finding.[^1]
rows: Tech firms: software, IT, data, research and development
Non-tech operating firms: manufacturing, finance, health, trade, transport, construction
ownData.note: Source: Zavient count in the JobsPipe job-ad index, pulled 26 Nov 2026, for six AI and machine learning engineer titles.[^3][^4] Counts are approximate, reposts are not removed, and 1,157 ads with no known size are left out. An ad is not a hire, and staffing agencies may recruit for clients of any size.

watchOuts: Hiring before picking the problem: RAND's most common root cause is a misunderstood or miscommunicated problem.[^16] Fix: name the workflow and its measure before you write a job ad.[^19]

One hire, no usable data: Gartner expects 60% of AI projects without AI-ready data to be abandoned through 2026.[^20][^16] Fix: check data access on a real sample and name a business owner first.[^17]
The empty seat: technical roles take a median 75 days to first fill, against 39 days for nonexecutive roles overall.[^10][^8] Fix: start the first workflow with outside help while you recruit.
Outside help that never hands over. Fix: write runbooks, test data and training into the contract as milestones.[^17]

Pilots that stall: Gartner predicted 30% of generative AI projects would be dropped after a trial build (proof of concept) by end of 2025.[^21] Fix: set a go-or-stop date and a dollar measure at the start.[^15]

A lone engineer with no domain help: RAND found data scientists rely on subject-matter experts to know what the data means.[^16] Fix: pair the hire with the ops lead from day one, so the team shapes the work.
howToTest: Write down today's numbers for one workflow: time per item, error rate and monthly cost.[^19]
Ask the advisor or candidate to restate your problem in your words before naming any tool.[^16]
Ask whether the first version needs AI at all. Google's first rule: don't be afraid to launch without machine learning.[^19]
Hold back recent real cases the builder never sees, such as last month's, and test on those.
Compare the AI-assisted output with your best person's work on the same cases. Count errors, not demos.
Price the lift: hours saved times loaded cost per hour, minus the cost to run it. BLS puts benefits at 31.5% of pay costs for professional and management staff.[^7]
Ask who owns the system after day 90, and get the answer in writing.[^17]
Agree a go-or-stop date before the pilot starts. Mid-market top performers reached full use in about 90 days.[^15]

faq.q: How much does an AI engineer cost?
faq.a: About $205,000 to $275,000 a year with benefits, by our math from BLS pay for the closest occupation at the median and 75th percentile.[^5][^6][^7] WTW says AI and machine learning engineers commonly get base pay premiums of 15% to 20%.[^12] Recruiting comes on top: SHRM's median is $1,200 a hire, and one AI recruiter illustrates agency fees of 20% to 25% of base.[^9][^11]

faq.q: Should I hire full-time or use outside help?
faq.a: Start with outside help on one workflow, and hire once you know what works.[^14] Few firms hire first: 1.3% of AI-using firms hired AI-trained staff.[^2][^1]

faq.q: Consulting firm or an in-house AI team: which makes more sense financially?
faq.a: Outside help makes more financial sense for a 40-500 person firm's first workflows; hire in-house once AI work fills a full-time role.[^14] One engineer costs about $205,000 to $275,000 a year with benefits, by our math from BLS pay data.[^5][^7] Partner-led pilots also reached deployment about twice as often in MIT's study, a correlation, not proof.[^15]

faq.q: Who owns the AI system after outside help leaves?
faq.a: Name an internal owner before work starts, and put knowledge transfer in the contract as milestones.[^17]

faq.q: How long does it take to hire an AI engineer?
faq.a: Plan on about six to eleven weeks with the seat empty. SHRM's median for nonexecutive roles is 39 days; Ashby's for technical roles is 75 days.[^8][^10]

pickElse: The gain is everyday tool use, not a custom system: train the staff you have instead (shape 3).[^1] By our math, training is more than ten times as common as hiring for AI.[^2]
Three or more use cases are queued and your data sits in one place: hire an AI lead now.[^14] Use outside help only to scope the first quarter.
A packaged product already does the job: buy it. Menlo Ventures, an investor, found 76% of enterprise AI use cases are bought, not built.[^22]
You need free help to start: try a Small Business Development Center, or a NIST MEP center if you make things.[^23][^24]

sources.name: MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (Jul 2025)
sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

offer.heading: Not sure whether to hire, bring in help, or both?
offer.body: Start with outside help on one workflow, then hire a lead to own it once it works. In a free 30-minute call, bring the workflow and what it costs today. You leave knowing whether it needs a hire, outside help or neither.

reviews.notes: The title asks which comes first, but the order was the fourth bullet; moved 'Prove one workflow first, then hire a lead' to the top. 'Operating firms' read as jargon in the bottom line; now 'non-tech firms your size', and the table row says the same. The BLS cost range and the honest 'not like for like' line on Zavient's prices are what I'd forward to the CEO.

NIST and 'proof of concept' appeared with no explanation; NIST is now glossed as the US standards body and proof of concept as a trial build. The hold-out step didn't say which cases; it now says last month's. Every flow step names a role, so I can hand each recipe to the people in it.

Wanted to know if one site can go first; recipe 2's rollout step now starts at one site or team. Pricing the lift as hours saved times loaded cost, minus run cost, is the margin view I need, and the BLS benefit share makes the loaded cost checkable. The job-ad table tells me peers my size are not hiring this role yet, which lowers the pressure to hire first.

Read as the head whose team would work with the hire. My worry is a builder who works around my people; watch-out 6 covers it, and recipe 1 now has me naming one subject-matter expert for the pilot, as RAND's domain-knowledge finding suggests. Front-line staff checking output before it reaches a customer is the right line for my team.

Steve wants a price and gets one: BLS cost of a hire, and Zavient's Sprint and advisory, labelled plainly as not like for like. He won't know a workflow's exact cost, so the offer now asks for a rough idea. Recipe 1 fits firms under about 150 staff, and the 'when not to hire help' list gives him free SBDC and MEP routes, which builds trust.

answers.walk-away: You should leave with one priced workflow, a before-and-after measure, a working pilot with a go-or-stop date, a job spec if needed, and a written handover[^16][^19].
answers.human-role: Your people keep the decisions: the ops lead owns the measure, the COO signs off on go-live, front-line staff check output, and a named owner runs it afterward[^17][^18].
answers.recipes: Prove one workflow before hiring if you have no engineers, bring in help if you have some IT, and train your team for everyday tasks.[^14][^1]
answers.what-goes-wrong: Most pilots stall because nobody pinned down the problem, the data isn't ready, or no one owns the system after the build[^16][^20].
answers.benchmark: Judge an advisor on your own numbers: record today's baseline, test on real cases they never saw, price the lift, and get the owner and go-or-stop date in writing[^19][^7].
answers.something-else: Skip outside help when the gain is everyday tool use, when three or more queued use cases justify an AI lead, or when a packaged product does the job[^1][^14][^22].
answers.own-data: Giants do: non-tech firms of 51 to 500 staff posted about 125 US AI-engineer ads in 30 days, against 1,262 from the largest firms in the same sectors[^3].
